name: Cylon
workload: Distributed groupby/join/aggregation operators over a uniformly random two-int64-column, 10^9-row dataset (worst-case for key-based ops), run at increasing parallelism (1-512 cores) across a 15-node cluster, compared to serial pandas and to Dask/Modin.
claimed_speedup: Paper states Cylon's C++ local operators 'perform on par or better than pandas' at parallelism=1, and Figure 3 plots dotted lines for speed-up over pandas (pandas_time/time) that increase with core count; exact per-point multipliers are shown only in log-scale figures, not as a single quoted number in the text.
compiler_and_flags: GCC v9.4, OpenMPI v4.1, Apache Arrow v5.0; explicit optimization flags (e.g. -O level) not stated
hardware: 15-node Intel Xeon Platinum 8160 cluster, 255GB RAM/node, SSD storage, Infiniband 40Gbps interconnect, up to 40 of 48 cores/node used
tradeoffs: Needs an MPI/UCX/Gloo runtime and a distributed cluster to realize the shown gains; pandas operator coverage was only ~25% at publication; the documented public interface is mostly the Python binding (pycylon) even though the core engine (libcylon) is C++.
caveats: Speedups are shown as log-scale plots (pandas_time/time) rather than a tabulated headline number, so exact multipliers can't be quoted verbatim from the page. Dask and Modin are explicitly called out as 'compared here only as a baseline' rather than tuned competitors, so the pandas comparison (not Dask/Modin) is the load-bearing claim. Venue is a Euro-Par-adjacent workshop paper, not full peer review of a top DB venue.
found_via: arXiv search 'Cylon dataframe' (HN/arXiv fallback per harness, package-registry search yielded no direct hits), then opened arxiv.org/abs/2209.06146 and cylondata/cylon repo

name: Hydra Columnar (Postgres columnar extension)
workload: ClickBench-derived 42-query suite over a 100M-row (80GB) dataset ('clickbench-100M') and a TPC-H-like 10GB 'warehouse-10G' suite, run inside PostgreSQL comparing Hydra's columnar table access method against vanilla Postgres heap tables.
claimed_speedup: README chart 'FasterthanPG.png' shows Hydra's columnar storage consistently faster than vanilla Postgres across the ClickBench 42-query set; exact per-query multipliers exist only in the linked chart image and Bencher.dev dashboards, not as machine-readable numbers in the page text, so no number is quoted here.
hardware: AWS c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GiB RAM) with 500 GiB GP2 storage for release benchmarks; GitHub-hosted 4-core runners for continuous benchmarks
tradeoffs: It is a Postgres extension, not a standalone embeddable library; speed gains apply only to tables explicitly created with Hydra's columnar access method, not to Postgres workloads generally. The project (originally 'hydradatabase/hydra') has since been renamed/consolidated into 'hydradatabase/columnar' with no commits in over a year.
caveats: The baseline actually beaten in the README's own chart is vanilla PostgreSQL, not one of the five named incumbents (Arrow/DuckDB/ClickHouse/pandas/polars). The repo also runs the ClickBench suite, which does include DuckDB and ClickHouse among its ~40+ tested engines, but no page text claims Hydra beats those two -- only Postgres. Because the headline numbers live in externally-hosted chart images/Bencher.dev graphs rather than quotable text, and compiler/flags are unstated, tier is capped at C.
found_via: GitHub search 'topic:olap language:C++' surfaced hydradatabase/hydra (redirects to hydradatabase/columnar); opened README.md and BENCHMARKS.md
